summary: Specifies a way for a SIP user agent client to send one MESSAGE request to many destinations, through a SIP URI-list service. The client sends the payload together with a list of URIs to the service, which sends a MESSAGE request with the payload to every URI in the list. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Rather than texting each friend one by one, you send one text and a list of names to a helper. The helper then delivers a copy to everyone on the list.

how to send a sip message to multiple recipients
subtitle: Send one SIP instant message plus a list of recipients, and let a service deliver a copy to each of them.

tldr.problem: SIP MESSAGE requests, as defined in RFC 3428, have no way to send the same instant message to several recipients or to reply to all of them.
tldr.mechanism: The sender puts a recipient-list body and the message in one MESSAGE request to a MESSAGE URI-list service. The service sends a separate MESSAGE to each URI and can add a recipient-list-history body so receivers can Reply-To-All.
tldr.outcome: Group pager-mode messaging works without setting up a session. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC.

today: RFC 5365 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on RFC 5363 and RFC 5364.

sections.title: The Group Messaging Problem
sections.content:
SIP-based messaging in RFC 3428 has no mechanism for sending the same request to multiple recipients or for replying to all recipients. RFC 5365 states two requirements. REQ-1: a user must be able to send an instant message to multiple recipients. REQ-2: the recipient of a group message MUST be able to send a message to all other participants (Reply-To-All).

Setting up a session, for example with MSRP, is one option, but sometimes the sender just wants to send a small pager-mode message to an ad hoc group without the burden of a session. This RFC covers that case.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you just want to shout one quick message to a few friends, without setting up a whole group call first.

sections.title: The MESSAGE URI-List Service
sections.content:
A MESSAGE URI-list service is a specialized URI-list service that receives a MESSAGE request with a URI list and sends a similar MESSAGE request to each URI in it. Some header fields may change, but the instant message payload is not changed. These services behave effectively as specialized B2BUAs.

The sending UAC must be configured with the SIP URI of the service. Discovering and provisioning that URI is outside the scope of the RFC. The RFC also defines incoming MESSAGE request (UAC to service), outgoing MESSAGE request (service to each recipient's UAS) and Reply-To-All.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper is like a post office clerk. You hand over one letter and a list of addresses, and the clerk makes the copies and delivers them.

sections.title: How a Group Message Flows
sections.content:
The UAC builds a MESSAGE with a multipart body: a list of URIs formatted as a resource list document (RFC 4826) extended with the attributes of RFC 5364, plus the instant message. Its Content-Disposition is recipient-list, as specified in RFC 5363.

The service creates one MESSAGE per listed recipient, copies the payload into each, and attaches a new URI list whose Content-Disposition is recipient-list-history. That list contains the non-anonymous to and cc targets, so recipients learn who else got the message and can reply to them. Each target can be tagged with copyControl (to, cc or bcc) and an anonymize attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk writes everyone's name on each copy, except for people who asked to stay secret.

sections.title: Rules for the Sender
sections.content:
The UAC formats the request per RFC 3428 Section 4, puts the service's SIP or SIPS URI in the Request-URI and adds the recipient-list body. It MUST include the recipient-list-message option-tag in a Require header field. UAs able to process such requests SHOULD list the tag in Supported when answering OPTIONS.

The default list format is the flat resource list from RFC 4826 with copy control attributes; UAs SHOULD use flat lists and SHOULD NOT use <entry-ref>. A UAC may use the "?" mechanism of RFC 3261 to ask the service to add a header field, but MUST NOT use the special body hname.

The service answers the UAC with 202 (Accepted). That says only that it will try to deliver. It says nothing about whether the copies arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: You must clearly tell the clerk that this is a group letter, and you give a simple flat list of names.

sections.title: What the Service Does
sections.content:
The service finds the recipients in the URI list and MUST follow RFC 5363 on duplicate URIs so no one gets duplicates. For each recipient it builds a new MESSAGE following RFC 3428 Section 4. The From header field MUST match the incoming one, subject to privacy requirements. It SHOULD set a new To header field to the recipient's URI and SHOULD create a new Call-ID, a separate CSeq count and a fresh Max-Forwards value. It MUST add its own Via value.

P-Asserted-Identity and Authorization handling have detailed rules based on trust and realm. For bodies, the service MUST NOT copy security bodies addressed to itself, SHOULD copy the remaining bodies, and MUST remove the multipart/mixed wrapper if only one body is left. When it includes a URI list it MUST set Content-Disposition to recipient-list-history with a handling parameter of optional, and SHOULD encrypt the list with the receiver's public key using S/MIME. It MUST generate only MESSAGE requests and ignore any method parameter in listed URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk copies the sender's name onto each letter, uses a fresh tracking number, and puts only one message in each envelope.

sections.title: Receivers and Security
sections.content:
A receiving UAS behaves as in RFC 3428 Section 7. If it supports this RFC and sees a recipient-list-history body, it can learn the AORs of the other intended recipients and create a reply (for example a MESSAGE or INVITE) to the sender and the rest.

Implementations MUST follow the security rules of RFC 5363, which include opt-in lists and mandatory authentication and authorization of clients. For private content, the UAC SHOULD use S/MIME: encrypt the message body with a content encryption key, then encrypt that key with each receiver's public key and attach it.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers can see who else got the message and answer everyone. For secrets, you lock the message so only the right people can open it.
